server/remote-access.js.about: The addresses a paired device is refused, each with the reason it needs a person at the PC.
The address a paired device loads a widget's files from: the key sits in the path because the cookie cannot go there, and this reads it back out.
Says whether the Host and Origin a paired device sent name this PC: an IP address the PC holds now, or its own HTTPS name, and lists the addresses a device can pair at.
The secrets of a paired device: its token and how it is hashed and compared, the pairing code a person types, and the cookie that carries the token.
Limits how often one address or one paired device may ask, and how many requests a dashboard load is allowed.
The saved list of paired devices as it is read back from disk: each record cleaned, and the part of a device the settings page may see.
Keeps the paired devices: pairing with a code, looking a device up by its token, renaming, revoking, and forgetting one that has not come back for a long time.

server/claude-bridge.js.about: How long the live Claude Code bridge waits and how much it keeps: time limits and size caps for sessions, approvals, questions and follow-ups.
Clamps what Claude Code sends before it is kept or drawn: a trimmed string, a finite number, a percentage, the project's folder name.
Turns a tool call of Claude Code into what the tile shows: a one-line summary, the changed lines of an edit, the plan's to-do list.
A question or a plan Claude Code asks about: the card the tile draws for it, and the answer handed back to the session in the tool's own shape.
Says how loudly a tool call of Claude Code must be asked about: destructive commands, publishing, the network, files outside the project, and prompts Claude Code wrote itself.
What the Xenon mod inside Claude Code reports: the key of an approval it handed back, and its usage measure as the status the tile reads.

server/claude-usage.js.about: What Claude Code usage would cost at API prices: the price table per model and the cost of one usage record.
The Claude plan the user picked for the usage tile: the presets, the cleaned setting and the weekly budget it gives.
Turns the lines of a Claude Code transcript into usage records, the prompts a person typed and the session's summary.
Adds the usage records of every Claude Code session up into what the usage tile shows: today, this week, per project, per day, and what is running now.

server/claude-transcript.js.about: Finds the transcript file of a Claude Code session by its id inside Claude Code's own projects folder, and remembers the answer for a while.
Reads the messages out of a stretch of a Claude Code transcript: the text a person or Claude wrote, the pictures, the slash commands and the tool calls of each turn.

server/claude-run.js.about: Finds the folder a Claude Code project works in, read from the start of its newest transcript, and says whether a path is a folder.
The two answers the Claude Code runner works out once and remembers: where the program is, and which options it accepts.
Finds the Claude Code program on this computer without a shell, and reads from its own --help which options it accepts.
The text the Claude Code runner takes in and shows: control characters stripped and a length kept, the short id of a project folder, and the one line that says what a tool call touches.
How much a run started from the dashboard may take: prompt, output, projects, folders, time and the efforts a run can ask for.
Where a run may start: the projects Claude Code already worked in, read from its transcripts, and the folders added by hand.
What a run's stream of events leaves in its record: the text said, the session, the cost and the tool calls with how they ended.

server/linux-collectors.js.about: The small tools every Linux reader uses: run a command, read a text file, split lines, tell a number, do several things a few at a time.
Linux graphics card readings in the shape gpu.ps1 gives: what nvidia-smi prints, and for AMD and Intel what the kernel says under /sys/class/drm.
Linux disks in the shapes the Windows readers give: the drives df lists, and each disk's reads, writes and temperature from /proc/diskstats and sysfs.
What /sys/class/hwmon says on Linux: the processor's temperature and clock, the fans, and one reading of any sensor file for the sensor catalog.
The Linux network reading in the shape network.ps1 gives: ping to 1.1.1.1 and the bytes of each real interface from /proc/net/dev.
The open windows of an X11 session on Linux, read with wmctrl, xdotool and xprop, and how one is brought forward or closed.
Linux sound through PipeWire: what pw-dump lists turned into the rows the volume mixer draws, and which node a volume command is aimed at.
Turns a key combination into the arguments ydotool takes on Linux.
How long nobody has touched a Linux PC, from logind or xprintidle.

server/darwin-collectors.js.about: The small tools every macOS reader uses: run a command and fail, run one and get nothing on failure, split lines, tell a number.
Reads temperatures, graphics load and processor clock out of what macmon and Xenon's own macOS helper print.
macOS disks in the shapes the Windows readers give: the volumes df and mount list, and each disk's reads and writes from ioreg.
The macOS network reading in the shape network.ps1 gives: ping and the bytes of each real interface from netstat.
The open apps of a Mac for the app switcher: the list System Events or the helper gives, cleaned, and the osascript calls that ask and quit.
macOS sound as the rows the volume mixer draws: the volume settings and the devices system_profiler lists, with stand-ins while the list is read.
The running programs of a Mac with their processor time and memory, read from ps.
Whether macOS lets Xenon read the user's protected folders (Full Disk Access), and whether a folder is inside the home folder.
How long nobody has touched a Mac, and the Mac's own id, both read from ioreg.

server/ai-local.js.about: What the local assistant can be set to: the providers, the Ollama models offered and the ones that see pictures, the Ollama address, and the voice for a language.
Whether this PC can run a local model: the memory each model needs, and a reading of this PC's memory and graphics memory.
Translates between the assistant's Gemini-shaped tools and history and what Ollama takes and answers.
The calls to a running Ollama: a chat turn on either of its endpoints, whether it answers, the installed models, what a model can do, and a model download.
One chat turn of the assistant on a local Ollama model, with its tool calls, and a second try on a smaller model when the first one crashes the graphics card.
Speech to text on this PC with whisper.cpp: where its program and model are, how a recording is prepared, and the cleaned transcript.
Finds the Ollama program on this PC, starts it, and switches its start at login on or off.
Fetches a DuckDuckGo results page for the free web search and reads the results out of its HTML.
Installs whisper.cpp when the user asks for local speech to text: the pinned download on Windows, Homebrew on macOS.

server/ai-cli.js.about: The limits of the assistant's subscription providers (Claude Code, Codex): which they are, how long a turn may take, how much text is kept, and what a model name may look like.
Finds the Codex program on this PC when it is not on the PATH: the folders it installs into and the newest copy among them.
Runs the Claude Code or Codex program once for the assistant: a clean environment, a time limit, capped output, and a second try without a flag an older version does not know.
Reads what Claude Code and Codex print about themselves: the version, whether the user is signed in, and the models they offer.
Turns the assistant's conversation into the one prompt a command-line provider takes, with the newest pictures in the form each program accepts.
Offers Xenon's tools to a command-line provider over MCP for the length of one turn: the turn's session, the calls it answers, and the tools in the shape MCP lists them.
Reads the answer of a Claude Code or Codex turn out of what the program printed, and says so when the user is not signed in.

server/ai-knowledge.js.about: What the assistant knows about Xenon itself: the written topics it looks up to answer how the app works.

server/ai-models.js.about: Picks a provider's model: what a stored choice means, one cleaned entry of a provider's model list, and the newest model of a family.
Reads the list of Ollama models Xenon offers to download: the fetch with its size and time limits, and each entry cleaned.

server/ai-anthropic.js.about: Translates the assistant's Gemini-shaped tools and history into what the Anthropic API takes.
One call to the Anthropic API with the user's own key, and its failure as an error the assistant can show.
The Claude models the user's Anthropic key can use, each sorted into its family.

server/ai-openai.js.about: One call to the OpenAI API with the user's own key, and its failure as an error the assistant can show.
The models the user's OpenAI key can use, each sorted into what it is for.

server/wakeword.js.about: Cuts the microphone's sound into stretches of speech for the wake word: how loud counts as speech, when a stretch ends, and the stretch as a WAV file.
Says whether what was heard is the wake word, under the assistant's name or its old one.

server/bit-messages.js.about: Cleans one message Bit is asked to show before it is kept: its limits, its text, its time, its button and its picture.

server/web-push.js.about: The cryptography of Web Push: the VAPID keys and the signed token (RFC 8292), and the encrypted payload (RFC 8291).
A phone's push subscription as it is accepted and kept: a public HTTPS endpoint, its keys, and the saved list cleaned.
Sends one encrypted notification to a browser's push service and says whether the subscription is gone.

server/embedded-browser.js.about: Finds a Chromium browser on this PC for the browser tile: the places Edge, Chrome and the others install to on each system.
Turns what a person typed in the browser tile's bar into an address: a site when it looks like one, a search otherwise.
Turns a touch, click, wheel or key from the browser tile into the command the browser's debugging protocol takes.
The two scripts the browser tile runs in every page before the page's own: one hides that the browser is driven, one reports whether the page plays sound.
How big and how often the browser tile's picture is drawn: the frame rate cap, the size limits and the sharpness for a small tile.
Looks after the browser tile's own profile folder: ends a browser left over from a crash, clears its locks, and starts the profile over when it was spoiled.
Starts the hidden browser behind the browser tile with its command line, reads the port it listens on, and ends it with everything it started.

server/discord-rpc.js.about: Signing Xenon in to the Discord app on this PC: the addresses, the permissions asked for, and a failed sign-in said plainly.
The small sums behind the Discord voice controls: a switch flipped, push-to-talk toggled, a volume nudged, and one person's volume.
What the Discord app sends turned into what the tile draws: the people in a voice channel with their pictures, soundboard sounds, and notifications.
The local pipe to the Discord app: where it is, that it belongs to this user, and the framing of each message sent and read.
The optional log of what the Discord app sends, switched on for a diagnosis.

server/codex-appserver.js.about: Talks JSON-RPC with Codex's own app server over its pipes: lines put back together, one request with its time limit, and an answer that means not supported.
Clamps a value Codex sent before it is kept: a trimmed string, a whole number, a percentage.
Reads Codex's answers about the account: who is signed in, the plan limits and credits, the usage per day, the hooks installed and the version.
Reads Codex's recent work: the list of threads with their state, and the messages of one thread with the text a person typed cleaned.

server/linux-index.js.about: Answers a file search from the Linux file index: how well a name matches what was typed, and the matches in order.
What the Linux file index says about disk space: the overview of a drive by kind of file, and the contents of one folder with sizes.

server/ics-feeds.js.about: Reads the text of an iCalendar file (RFC 5545) into events: folded lines, dates with their time zone, escaped text.
Works out when a repeating calendar event happens inside a stretch of days, from its RRULE.
The calendar feeds a user saved: the list cleaned, and each address kept on the PC while only its host name goes to the page.

server/sdk-widgets.js.about: What a widget can see and do: the SDK version, the live streams it may subscribe to, the actions it may ask for by category, and the limits on what an action may carry.
The shapes a widget package's names must have: its id, the ids inside it, its entry file, a path segment, and the file types it may ship.
The Content-Security-Policy a widget's frame is served with: the sandbox's kill-switch, and the same policy opened to this PC's own address for a paired device.
How much a widget's manifest may declare: its size, the number of packages scanned, and the caps on hosts, hooks, macros, states and key handlers.
Checks a request a widget sends through Xenon's fetch proxy: the host it may reach, never this PC or a private network unless the user said so, and the methods and headers allowed.
Cleans the parts of a widget's manifest one by one: text and lists, the hosts it asks for and the ones the user fills in, hooks, and what a key handler takes.
The two scripts Xenon puts into every widget's page under reserved names: the performance probe and the guard that turns WebRTC off.
The files of a widget package: which file a request for an asset may reach, its type, and the files read back for sharing within their size limits.
Puts a widget package in place: the staged swap an update uses, where a package came from and whether it may be shared on, and what an overwrite keeps.

server/sdk-asset-cache.js.about: Decides what the widgets' picture cache keeps: the size and count limits per package and in all, the name a cached file gets, and which files go first.

server/football.js.about: Cleans single values of the football data: an id, the API key, a number, a picture address, a colour, a season, the state of a match.
The football widget's saved settings: the followed teams and the defaults, cleaned.
Fetches JSON from the football service with a size cap and a total deadline, a few requests at a time.
Reads one match out of what the football service answers: the teams, the score, the time and the state.
Looks teams up at the football service: a search by name, and a team's badge, colours and ground.
Remembers the last score of each match so a goal or a final whistle is announced once.

server/news.js.about: Reads the headlines out of an RSS or Atom feed without a parser library: tags found by hand, entities decoded, markup stripped, sizes capped.
Fetches a news feed's text from a public address only, with a size cap and a total deadline, a few feeds at a time.
The language and country a news search is asked in, and the Google News address for a topic.

server/stocks.js.about: The stocks widget's saved settings: the watchlist, the data provider and the defaults, cleaned.
Fetches JSON from a market data service with a size cap and a total deadline, a few requests at a time.
Reads a quote and its small chart out of what Yahoo Finance answers.
Remembers each symbol's last move so a price alert is announced once.

server/community-messages.js.about: Cleans one message the Xenon hub publishes before the app shows it: who it is for, its button, its picture or video, its poll, and the allowed hosts for each.
Says which of the hub's messages are showing today: each one's first and last day.
Fetches the hub's messages file, only when it changed, with a size cap and a total deadline.

server/fpsmon.js.about: Reads PresentMon's output: the columns of its header, one row as values, which programs are not games, and how a game is presenting its frames.
Turns the frame times kept for a program into what the dashboard shows: its frames per second, its frame statistics, and the frames since a moment.
What the FPS reader remembers while it runs: its PresentMon child, whether it is paused or stopped, and how its last starts went.
The frames the FPS reader keeps for each process PresentMon reports: the entry of a process, the rows added to it, and a PresentMon stream cut into rows.
The names of Xenon's own ETW sessions for PresentMon, and how a session that a killed PresentMon left behind is stopped.

server/linux-fps.js.about: Reads MangoHud's log files on Linux: the columns, the newest rows as frames per second, the program a log belongs to, and Xenon's lines merged into its config.

server/file-transfer.js.about: What kind of file a transferred file is: the closed list of types served as themselves, the ones always served as a plain download, and the ones that get a thumbnail.
The name of a transferred file: the label a person sees, never a path, the extension by shape, the name it is delivered under and the download header.
Delivers a received file into the folder the user chose on the PC: the folder checked, a free name found, and the file marked as coming from outside.
Writes an upload to disk as it arrives, counting its bytes against the size limit, and leaves nothing behind when it fails.

server/call-detect.js.about: The words in a notification that mean a call is ringing, that it is not, and that it is a video call, in the languages the apps use.
The apps whose notifications can be a call, with how each is named and what it can be asked to do.

server/calls.js.about: What can be done with a ringing call from the dashboard, per app and system, and the call as the page sees it.
What the phone-call relay remembers while the engine runs: who gave it its helpers, the calls in progress, and the timer that drops old ones.
Starts and ends a ringing call for the phone-call relay: tells the dashboards, notifies the phone that is away, and drops a call nobody answered.
What a tap on a call card does: answer, decline or hang up, by bringing the calling app forward and sending it the key, or by asking the phone.

server/linux-phone.js.about: Asks BlueZ and oFono over D-Bus with busctl on Linux, and reads values and object lists out of its JSON answers.
Picks the paired phone and its modem out of what D-Bus lists on Linux, and reads the calls and their state.

server/auto-update.js.about: Decides whether an update may install itself now: a newer version, old enough, the PC idle, at night, and not marked as one to ask about.

server/lyrics.js.about: Cleans a track's title and artist before lyrics are looked up: video tags, remaster notes and featured artists out, and the searches to try in order.
Reads lyrics into lines: timed ones from the LRC format, and plain text.

server/codex-bridge.js.about: Turns a tool call of Codex into what the tile shows: a one-line summary, the files a patch touches, and how loudly it must be asked about.

server/linux-hotkey.js.about: Turns a key combination into the accelerator GNOME understands, reads what gsettings prints about shortcuts, and writes the command the desktop runs on the shortcut.

server/version-ping.js.about: What the anonymous version ping says and what is remembered of it: the day and week in UTC, the install's age as a bucket, the body sent, and the state kept after a ping.

server/menu-widgets.js.about: The choices of the menu's Add row: a tile, a package from the Store with its pictures, a key, and the filters over them.

server/community-catalog.js.about: How long a Store entry's description may be: the shared limit, or a fixed one when the shared file is not there.
Cleans the Store catalog the site publishes before the app trusts it: each entry's id, kind, version, pictures, price and limits, and which entries are showing.
Fetches a file of the Store catalog, only when it changed, with a size cap and a total deadline.

server/actions/registry.js.about: Which program a Deck key or the assistant may launch: the kinds of file that count as an application on each system, how a typed path is completed, and how the launch arguments are read. Part of the action registry: only registry.js requires this file.
Which files an action refuses to open because opening them runs code, and which scripts the runScript action may start, per system. Part of the action registry: only registry.js requires this file.

Checks of the small values an action carries: a web address, a percentage, a position in a track, a key combination, a Store app id, a Steam app id. Part of the action registry: only registry.js requires this file.

Finds the audio output an action names in the list of outputs that are connected now, for one device, a pair to switch between, or an ordered list. Part of the action registry: only registry.js requires this file.

server/actions/wavelink.js.about: Turns what Wave Link 2 and Wave Link 3 send into the same channels, mixes and outputs, with every volume as a percentage, and works out which mixes an action means.
Where Wave Link listens on this PC and how long to wait for it: the hosts and ports of both versions, the port file Wave Link 3 publishes, and the timings of the connection.

server/actions/home-assistant.js.about: The addresses of a Home Assistant server, worked out from the one the user typed, and the bounded download of a camera picture from it.
What the dashboard keeps of a Home Assistant entity, and the checks that tell an entity id, a camera and a media player.
Turns an action of a Deck key, a tile or the assistant into the Home Assistant service call that does it, refusing values a service would not take.
Cleans the Home Assistant settings as they are saved: entities, cameras and their angles, dashboards, and the token, which is kept on a save without one and never sent back to the screen.

server/actions/voicemeeter.js.about: What a Voicemeeter action may name and set: the editions with their strips and buses, the parameter names that are safe to send, the range of a gain, and where the Voicemeeter library is looked for.

server/actions/unifi.js.about: Cleans the UniFi Protect settings as they are saved: the address of the console, the cameras and their layout and angles, the alerts, and the sign-in, which is kept on a save without one and never sent back to the screen.

server/actions/streamerbot.js.about: Builds what is sent to Streamer.bot: the answer to its sign-in challenge, the arguments of an action, and the request an action of a Deck key becomes.
Turns an event Streamer.bot reports (a follow, a subscription, a donation, a raid) into the short activity line the dashboard shows.

server/actions/chroma.js.about: Turns a Chroma action into the effect the Razer Chroma service takes: the colour, the devices it goes to, and the grid of a keyboard.

server/remote-control/installer.js.about: Which package gives Sunshine and Tailscale on Windows, on each Linux package manager and on macOS, and the Windows services they install.
The oldest Sunshine that remote control works with, and how two version numbers are compared.
The account the server runs as, in the shell-safe shape a user name has, or nothing.
How a package is installed on each system: winget on Windows, Homebrew on macOS, and flatpak or the distribution's package manager on Linux.
How the version of the installed Sunshine is read on each system, and how an old one is upgraded with the package manager that installed it.

server/remote-control/tailscale.js.about: Reads what the Tailscale program says: the status of this PC on its network, its name there, a sign-in link, whether certificates are on, and whether an error means a missing right.
Where the Tailscale program is looked for on each system.

server/capabilities/layers.js.about: Finds what a layer request means: the widget it names, the one already placed, its page and its monitor, and how a placed widget is described back.
The keyboard shortcuts of the layers: how one is shown, how the overlay, menu and pad shortcuts are set, and the hint that tells which key brings the overlay up.
Moves, resizes and restyles a widget that is already placed on the desktop or in the overlay.

server/lighting-providers/hue.js.about: Talks to a Philips Hue bridge: plain requests, requests over TLS checked against the bridge's own certificate, and the id a bridge is known by.
Turns a red-green-blue colour into what a Hue light takes, in the old and in the new form of the bridge's interface.

server/perf-session/core-shield.js.about: The rules of the core shield: how many cores a process uses, which processes belong to one app, which are never moved, which app is in front and which are the busiest.

server/linux-media.js.about: What playerctl prints on Linux turned into the now-playing shape the media tile reads, and a media command as playerctl's arguments.

server/darwin-media.js.about: What the macOS now-playing reader prints turned into the shape the media tile reads, with the cover as a data address, and a media command as its arguments.

server/linux-mpris.js.about: Reads what MPRIS players answer over D-Bus on Linux: their names, one player's track and state, and which player is the one to show.

server/gamedetect.js.about: The programs that are never a game, even in full screen or with many frames: launchers, browsers, players and tools.

server/remote-https.js.about: Why the HTTPS door for paired devices is not up, as one of a few reasons the settings page turns into a sentence.

server/winnotif.js.about: What the notification reader remembers while it runs: its child process, what it has read so far, and how its last starts went.
One notification as the child reader printed it, turned into the shape the dashboards get: known keys only, lengths capped, and an id the server gives.
What the notification reader is asked from outside while its child runs: stop the child and forget what it read, look less often through a game, and say what state it is in.

server/supporter-redeem.js.about: What the redeem proxy remembers while the engine runs: this install's id, the trial pass and the rating votes it was given.
One HTTPS POST of JSON to the supporter hub, with a deadline and a limit on how much of the answer is read.
The shapes the redeem proxy accepts before it asks the hub: a code in its canonical form, an entry id, a key version and a version number.

What this install keeps in the data folder for the supporter hub: its own id, made once, the hashes of it that go out, one for each purpose so the hub cannot tie one to another, and the remembered supporter pass.

server/ai-xenon-credits.js.about: What the Sparks client remembers while the engine runs: its session with the hub and the last balance the hub told it.
The models and effort levels a turn paid with Sparks may use, how long and how large one round may be, when a busy round is asked again, and the errors of the hub that are passed on.
The Sparks client's session with the hub: the saved pass or Sparks code turned into a token, asked for again before it ends or when the hub stops taking it, and one hub call made with it.
Which rounds of a turn paid with Sparks are handed from the chat model to the creation model, and the tools the creation model gets.

server/guardian.js.about: How often the sensor history samples and writes, how much it keeps, and when it warns.
The metrics the sensor history keeps, how a reading goes into a bucket, and how buckets are averaged.
The sensor history's store: read from disk once and made safe, written whole, handed to and taken from a backup.
What the sensor history counts: a reading into its hour and day, the seconds of the app in front, and a warning when something runs hot.
What the sensor history answers when it is asked: the charts, the energy, one metric over time and the digest.

server/diskspace.js.about: The limits of the disk space module: how long a scan and a delete may take, and how much is listed, hashed and deleted at a time.
What the disk space module may delete: the guard's view of this machine, a path looked at again just before it goes, and whether anything here can put a file in the bin.
The drives and volumes the disk space module can offer as places to index, asked for without holding a request and remembered for a while.

Looking inside an overview: the ids that stand for its folders and files, the overview as the browser gets it, one folder opened, and a file shown in its folder. A path never comes in from the browser.
The full scan through the helper: started and stopped, what came back sorted into the categories, same-size files proven duplicates, and the summary kept for the next start.
The last overview of each drive and the drive's history, kept on disk: read once, written a little after they change, and shown marked as old while the index cannot answer yet.
One cleanup as it runs: each item checked again and put in the bin a batch at a time, a folder in use opened up, the progress told as it goes, and the helper call behind every delete.
A cleanup asked for: the items found again by their ids, each one passed by the guard, and the job started; and a folder emptied into the bin for the Deck.
The overview of one drive built from the living index: sizes, categories, kinds, old files and duplicates, reused while it is fresh, with today's point in the drive's history.
What the disk space module says of itself: the state the widget draws, and the figures Bit may read and explain.
Reads the folders a Linux desktop names in user-dirs.dirs, so that a Documents folder with a translated name is protected like the English one.

server/server.js.about: What the engine answers about the lights: the state of the lighting, its devices, the album colours, an event, the download page and the install of the iCUE kit, and SignalRGB.
What the engine answers for the stocks, football and news tiles: charts, standings, headlines and the searches.
What the engine answers for the Deck: its sounds, the icon of a program, the Store apps a key can open, the saved Deck, the states scripts set and whether the page shortcuts are held.
What the engine answers about the assistant: a turn and its stop, the command line assistants, the local models, the balance, an action on the PC and the chime.
What the engine answers about a Claude Code session: its transcript, a picture from it, an agent and the plan.
What the engine answers about sound: whether the levels are read, the watch and the programs that play.
What the engine answers about its version and the install of the app window.
What the engine answers about game mode and the performance screen.
What the engine does for the PC itself: turning the sensors on, locking the session and opening the macOS disk access settings.
What the engine answers about the open windows, and the install of the ad filter of the browser tile.
What the engine answers about opening the dashboard at sign-in.
What the engine takes from a widget: the answer to a Deck call and the states of its keys.
What the engine answers about itself: that it is up, and a line a page asks it to log.
What the engine answers about the screens of the PC.
What the engine does to open Discord.
What the engine answers about the shortcut of the search bar.
What the engine answers about the Store: the catalog, what is installed, the counts, the messages, a code, the limited items and the ratings.
What the engine answers about a supporter and the Sparks: the saved key, an update of owned content, a purchase and the wallet.
What the engine answers when a phone asks to install the dashboard as an app.
What the assistant does when asked to look in the Store or to install something from it: the install only opens the usual review on the screen, where the user confirms.
What the assistant does when asked to close an app: one program by its exact name, never Windows' own or Xenon (ai-pc-apps.js decides).

What the engine does while a Claude Code session talks to it: an event from the session, its messages, a permission it asks for, a question, the end of a turn, the commands of the session, and the answer, reply or decision the user gives.

What the engine answers about Claude Code on this PC: the link and its removal, the projects, the commands, the history, a file attached, a run and its stop, a folder a run may start in, and the budget.
What the engine does for a widget while it runs: an answer from the assistant, a web address fetched for it, the values it saves and its secrets.
What the engine answers about the widgets that are installed: the list, a permission the user grants, an install, and a package the user marks as their own.

What the engine answers about what the assistant remembers and has done: its memory, the running summary of a long conversation, the list of its actions, undoing one, and a Deck action it proposed that the user approves or cancels.

What the engine answers about the voice and the messages of the assistant: speaking a text and stopping, the wake word, the models to choose from, the cost of a Game Companion look, and the messages behind its card.
What the engine answers for the vitals tile: its saved state, a reminder and what Bit can do on this PC to make it felt, the pop-up it shows, and a roast.
What the engine answers about files sent between the phone and the PC: the list, a thumbnail, opening, revealing and deleting one, undoing a delete, and the settings with the folder they land in.

What the engine answers about the phone: its state, contacts, calls and messages, sending a message, dialling, what a button of the call card does, and a made-up call that rings only when testing is turned on.
What the engine does about the devices paired with it: turning the access on, cancelling a pairing, redeeming a code, renaming a device, and revoking one or all of them.
What the engine answers about notifications sent to a paired device: the key, an unsubscribe, the status and a test.
What the engine answers when files are searched: the results, the recent ones, a thumbnail and an icon, opening and revealing a file, and the state of the index.

What the engine answers about the disks: the state of a scan and its overview, a folder revealed or browsed, a scan and a cleanup with their cancels, the advice of the assistant, the reads and writes per disk, and the space developer tools hold with its cleanup.

What the engine answers about the smart home: the state of Home Assistant, its entities, dashboards and cameras, a test and a service call, the entities the Deck watches, a history a widget asks for, and UniFi Protect.

What the engine does when the lighting is changed: an effect, a manual colour, an animation, the mode of a device, a scan, one device, the lights it drives directly with their layout and scan, and the Chroma link.
What the engine answers about updating itself: a notice that was read, where an update stands, preparing and applying it, the automatic update and its postponement, and what is new in this version.

What the engine answers about using the PC from another device: the status, the install, the Tailscale sign-in, the Sunshine setup, the PIN, the switch that cuts it off, turning it on, off or on demand, the screens, closing a session, and blocking or unblocking.
What the engine does for the keys of the Deck: a press, a shortcut step a dashboard takes, the Deck in a window of its own, a page shortcut pressed, an action run, and the Deck saved.
What the engine answers about icon packs and sound packs, and where the automatic update of widgets stands.
What the engine answers about what a supporter unlocks: a code redeemed, the trial pass, and the lyrics translation and developer cleanup features with their trial and unlock.
What the engine answers about Performance Mode: its numbers, the power plan, Core Shield, its saved state, the plan the assistant proposes, the recent processes, and one of its actions run.

What the engine answers about volume and the mixers: the audio state, lowering the volume while the assistant speaks and restoring it, the microphone and the speaker chosen, Wave Link and Voicemeeter.
What the engine answers for the timers, the notes and their lists, the calendar events and the tasks.

What the engine answers about Codex and the ChatGPT tile: the state and a thread, an event, a permission and its decision, the link and its removal, and the conversations of the tile with a question asked, cancelled or deleted.
What the engine answers for the football tile, and what it saves for the tickers: the teams, the news feeds and the stocks watchlist.

What the engine answers about captures: a screenshot of the screens or of one monitor, the capture settings and the folder picked for them, clips cut from the marks of a video, and a capture sent to the phone.

What the engine does for the second screen, slideshow, browser and windows tiles: what the second screen needs, its driver and display, the pictures of a slideshow and one uploaded, the state of the ad filter, a favourite app started, and a tile taking what the assistant asked to play.
What the engine does for the look of the dashboard: a background uploaded and a font uploaded.
What the engine does with a picture uploaded to decorate one tile.
What the engine answers about the settings: all of them with the secrets left out, the settings of one tile saved, and a backup exported, imported or saved to a file.
What the engine answers for streaming: the actions, triggers and globals of Streamer.bot, the sources of OBS, and the streaming setup saved.
What the engine answers about what is playing: the media state, the lyrics, their offset and their translation with its usage.
What the engine answers about the weather, and the weather setup saved.
What the engine answers about the PC: the system and network readings, the batteries of its devices and the history of its hardware health.
What the engine answers when the notifications tile starts: what is turned on and the notifications it holds.
What the engine answers to the windows that show widgets on the desktop: whether they are being edited, what the app window can draw, and their strings in the saved language.
What the engine answers about the Xenon menu: its sections, and whether it is open over the screen.
What the engine answers about drawing over the screen: whether the drawing sheet is open.
What the assistant does when asked to make a widget or to read one the user made: a new widget passes the same check as any widget that is installed, and nothing is granted to it here.

What the assistant does when asked to make a look, a layout or another share code: it reads what a code may hold, builds one and tries it against the import, and never applies it (the user sees the usual review).
What the assistant does when asked to remember something about the user, or to forget it: the facts stay on this PC.
What the assistant does when asked to open an app, a site or a document, to lock the PC, or to run a command on it: a command is only proposed here, and runs after the user approves it on the screen.
What the assistant does when asked to look something up on the web.
What the assistant does when asked to open the Deck in a window, or to do what a Deck key does: same check and same list of actions as a key press, and the risky ones wait for the user on a card.
What the assistant does when asked about the PC: its readings now and over time, one sensor, the batteries of the devices, the power drawn, and where the sensors are read from.
What the assistant does when asked about sound: the microphone, the volume of the PC or of one app, and which speakers or microphone are in use.
What the assistant does when asked to play, pause or skip what is playing, or to play something in a tile of the dashboard.
What the assistant does when asked about the lights of the PC: a colour, the effects, the animation, and the lights on or off.
What the assistant does when asked about the weather.
What the assistant does when asked about stocks, football or the news: prices, scores and tables, headlines, and the stocks, teams and feeds the user follows.
What the assistant does when asked to change a setting, or the model and the effort it creates with.
What the assistant does when asked to read or to write the notes.
What the assistant does when asked about the tasks: list, add, change, tick off, delete one or all.
What the assistant does when asked about the calendar: list the events, add, change, delete one or all.
What the assistant does when asked about timers and stopwatches: start, pause, resume, list, delete.
What the assistant does when asked to find a file on the PC or to open one it found: it gets and gives back ids, never a path.
What the assistant does when asked what fills the disks: it only reads.
What the assistant does when asked to drive a live stream: OBS, Twitch, the YouTube broadcast, Streamer.bot, each through the same list of actions as a Deck key.
What the assistant does when asked about the smart home: list what is there, switch something or start a scene, and never a lock, an alarm or a door.
What the assistant does when asked to vote something of the Store: the vote only counts after the user approves it on a card.
What the Twitch routes do: sign-in, the live stream, followed and top channels, emotes, search and chat.
What the YouTube routes do: sign-in, the broadcast and its title, privacy and stream key, playlists, search and chat.
What the Spotify routes do: sign-in and its return address, what is playing, the queue, playlists, devices and starting the app.
What starting to listen to the microphone does: it picks the device and starts the recording the answer is read from.
The still pictures of the cameras of the house: one from UniFi Protect, one from Home Assistant.
The captures kept on this computer: the list, a file, its small picture, its transcript, the export and the spots saved.
What the assistant does in a Discord voice call: mute, deafen, join and leave.
The page the engine answers with for the scene window: the animated background on a screen of its own.
What the engine answers about the AI that runs on this computer: whether it is there, fetching a model, installing Whisper.
What the assistant does when asked about Xenon itself: it answers from the facts written for it, not from a guess.
The pictures the engine fetches for a widget so its frame can show them from the engine's own address: map tiles kept in memory, artwork kept on disk.
